identification.summary: North Korean threat actor that Microsoft has tracked since 2020 [S1]. Microsoft first referenced it, under the earlier name CERIUM, in November 2020, when it ran COVID-19-themed spear-phishing against vaccine and treatment developers [S4][S5]. Microsoft says Ruby Sleet has made its phishing much more sophisticated over several years and has compromised aerospace and defense-related organizations [S1]. Its tradecraft includes signing malware with certificates stolen from victims, distributing backdoored VPN clients and installers, and a December 2023 software supply chain attack on a South Korean construction company [S1][S2].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft: tracked since 2020 [S1]. First publicly named by Microsoft (as CERIUM) on 2020-11-13 [S4][S5].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Ruby Sleet (formerly CERIUM) [S3][S6]. Microsoft's mapping lists CERIUM and VELVET CHOLLIMA as other names [S6]. VELVET CHOLLIMA is widely used in open sources as a CrowdStrike name for Kimsuky-related activity, which Microsoft tracks separately as Emerald Sleet; see gaps. Some third-party press equates Ruby Sleet with APT37/ScarCruft, but Microsoft's mapping does not list those names [S6].

attribution.sponsor: North Korea (DPRK). Microsoft lists the origin as North Korea [S6] and discusses Ruby Sleet among North Korean state actors [S1][S2][S3]. None of the cited sources names a specific DPRK organization as sponsor.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft vendor attribution to North Korea [S1][S3][S6]. No US government attribution or indictment naming Ruby Sleet or CERIUM was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence telemetry and reporting from 2020 to 2024 [S1][S2][S3][S4].

objectives: Intelligence collection. Microsoft says stolen aerospace and defense information may help North Korea understand missiles, drones and related technologies [S1]. Microsoft assesses that the motive behind North Korean activity in this period, Ruby Sleet included, is intelligence collection [S2]. Its 2020 targeting of COVID-19 vaccine developers suggests health-research collection [S4][S5]. Microsoft judged maritime technology research a high North Korean priority in late 2022 and early 2023, when Ruby Sleet targeted that sector [S3].

regions: Germany and Israel (arms manufacturers, with Diamond Sleet) [S3]
Canada, France, India, South Korea and United States (2020 COVID-19 vaccine targeting by the three named actors combined) [S4][S5]
targeting.notes: Microsoft reports Ruby Sleet and other North Korean groups targeting the same high-priority sectors at once (defense, maritime). Microsoft suggests the DPRK assigns several actor groups to meet high-priority collection requirements [S3]. The 2020 country list covers all targets of Strontium, Zinc and Cerium together and is not specific to Cerium [S5].

capabilities.summary: Increasingly sophisticated spear-phishing, including 2020 COVID-19 lures impersonating World Health Organization representatives [S1][S5]. It researches targets to learn what software they run and builds custom capabilities for specific targets [S1]. It signs malware with legitimate certificates stolen from compromised victims [S1]. It distributes backdoored VPN clients, installers and other legitimate software [S1]. It has run software supply chain compromises: in December 2023 it replaced a legitimate VeraPort program at a South Korean construction company with a version that contacts Ruby Sleet infrastructure [S1]. Microsoft separately describes this as likely use of a backdoored installer of a South Korean electronic document program [S2].

campaigns.name: COVID-19 vaccine researcher spear-phishing (as CERIUM)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft says CERIUM used COVID-19-themed spear-phishing, posing as WHO representatives, against vaccine and treatment developers. The same report covers Zinc and Strontium. Microsoft says most attempts were blocked.

campaigns.name: Maritime and defense sector targeting
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports Ruby Sleet, Diamond Sleet and Sapphire Sleet targeting maritime and shipbuilding organizations. It says Ruby Sleet and Diamond Sleet compromised two arms manufacturers in Germany and Israel.

campaigns.name: Russian aerospace research institute compromise
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports that Ruby Sleet compromised an aerospace research institute in Russia, amid wider North Korean targeting of Russian government and defense entities.

campaigns.name: VeraPort supply chain attack on South Korean construction company
campaigns.summary: Ruby Sleet replaced a legitimate VeraPort program at a South Korean construction company with a version that communicates with Ruby Sleet infrastructure. Microsoft also describes this as a likely backdoored installer of a South Korean electronic document program.

campaigns.name: CYBERWARCON disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft summarizes Ruby Sleet's growing phishing sophistication, its use of stolen certificates and backdoored VPN clients, and its successful compromises of aerospace and defense organizations.

diamond.adversary: North Korean state-linked operators tracked by Microsoft as Ruby Sleet (formerly CERIUM) [S1][S3][S6].
diamond.capability: Spear-phishing with tailored lures; malware signed with stolen certificates; backdoored VPN clients and installers; custom target-specific tools; software supply chain compromise (VeraPort) [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-controlled C2 that trojanized VeraPort software contacted [S1]. Code-signing certificates stolen from compromised organizations [S1]. Specific domains and IPs are not in the cited sources.
diamond.victim: Aerospace, defense, satellite and weapons-system organizations in the US and South Korea [S1][S2]. Arms manufacturers in Germany and Israel [S3]. A Russian aerospace research institute [S3]. Maritime and shipbuilding organizations [S3]. COVID-19 vaccine developers in 2020 [S4][S5]. A South Korean construction company used as a supply chain vector [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: DPRK collection requirements on missiles, drones and other military technology [S1]. Opportunistic collection on Russia during the war in Ukraine (Microsoft says this of North Korean actors generally) [S3]. Pandemic-era health research [S4].
diamond.technology: Trust in code-signing certificates and in South Korean security and enterprise software distribution (VeraPort, document software installers, VPN clients) [S1][S2].

gaps: Alias conflict: Microsoft's mapping lists VELVET CHOLLIMA under Ruby Sleet [S6], but open sources commonly use VELVET CHOLLIMA for Kimsuky (Microsoft's Emerald Sleet). CrowdStrike's own profile was not retrieved, so it is unresolved whether this mapping reflects a partial overlap.

Some third-party coverage equates Ruby Sleet with APT37/ScarCruft and links it to the DPRK Ministry of State Security (e.g., Malpedia and MISP galaxy entries). Those pages could not be opened, and Microsoft's mapping does not support the equivalence. Do not merge APT37 reporting into this record without primary confirmation.

The December 2023 VeraPort supply chain attack (Ruby Sleet, per Microsoft) is distinct from the widely reported 2020 VeraPort abuse that ESET attributed to Lazarus. The vendor report Microsoft linked for the 2023 event (its URL references Kimsuky) was not reviewed.
No MITRE ATT&CK group ID, malware family names or infrastructure IOCs were found for Ruby Sleet in the cited sources.
The Microsoft On the Issues posts [S4][S7] could not be fetched directly; their content is taken from search summaries and trade-press coverage [S5].
No public Ruby Sleet activity after 2024 was found; current operational tempo is unknown.
Which specific DPRK organization sponsors Ruby Sleet is not stated in any Microsoft source reviewed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (operational environment): Key cyber terrain includes aerospace, satellite, missile and UAS program data held by DoD, the defense industrial base and allied (ROK, German, Israeli) manufacturers. It also includes the software supply chain those organizations rely on: VPN clients, installers and Korean enterprise software [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 2 (effects): Code-signing trust and software update channels let the actor bypass allow-listing and reputation controls [S1]. STEP 3 (threat model): Target research leads to a tailored phish or trojanized legitimate installer, then signed malware, then persistence and collection of technical data [S1]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is continued spear-phishing and trojanized-software intrusions against US and ROK aerospace and defense firms to collect missile, drone and satellite technology [S1][S2]. MDCOA is a supply chain compromise of software widely deployed across ROK or coalition defense networks, giving broad access to US Forces Korea partners and the DIB [S1]. Candidate indicators: binaries signed with certificates belonging to unrelated or recently breached companies; modified VPN client or VeraPort-type installers contacting unfamiliar hosts; aerospace-themed lures aimed at engineers [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track revoked or stolen code-signing certificates and vendor notices of trojanized installers affecting software used on DoD and coalition networks [S1]. (2) Authorities: most victims are DIB firms and allied manufacturers, so response depends on DIB CS and partner-nation channels rather than DODIN authorities [S1][S3]. (3) Mission assurance: weapons, aerospace and satellite program offices should treat third-party installers and VPN clients as supply chain risk [S1]. (4) Coordination: the actor operates against ROK and Israeli targets and in parallel with other DPRK clusters on the same sectors, so coordinate with USFK, ROK partners and other DPRK-focused tracking to deconflict attribution [S2][S3].
